rv.q: Rachel O’Riordan’s sensitive production is not afraid to take its time and sit in its silences, allowing ruminative rhythms to play out.
That’s what makes this play beautiful: in defiance of its own title, it’s about what endures.
This kind of nicely observed writing needs fabulous playing to stop from feeling like nicely observed writing.
Sometimes the dialogue gives way to monologues on life and death that sit oddly against the domestic realism.
But Alfie and Julie’s dialogue and actions often feel wildly implausible in the context of a 90-minute realtime conversation, overly crammed with exposition and incident.
It's a quietly moving play that makes sense on its own – without quite having the narrative heft to clean up as a piece of drama in its own right.
Though both kind and astute, this is the most awkward play in the trilogy: an uneasy mixture of detail and declamation.
But overall this is a gentle, sad, valedictory piece of work about life and death, happiness and class, performed and directed with great subtlety.
Such perfect performances prove that this is an outstanding way of finishing a trilogy which encompasses all of life.
End works beautiful on all counts.
Owen and Reeves, at the top of their game, make the battle for a good death heartbreakingly poignant and fragile.
Overall, a thoughtful and poignant experience.
End falters in its reluctance to push further than gentle inquiry.

cn.t: David Eldridge's trilogy concludes with a poignant, tender exploration of love and mortality that critics find deeply moving. Anchored by Clive Owen and Saskia Reeves' performances, this intimate two-hander earns praise for its heartfelt emotional resonance.
